name: Simon
description: Of the tribe of Benjamin, made governor of the temple; fell out with Onias the high priest and told Apollonius the treasury was full of money that could be seized for the king; his faction's hatred led to murders, and his accusations against Onias continued after Heliodorus's failed seizure

points: But one Simon of the tribe of Benjamin, who was made governor of the temple, fell out with the high priest about disorder in the city. The role of the temple governor was read: management of temple resources, maintenance of the temple, administration of worship, handling disputes, coordination with other authorities, and security. Whatever the dispute was, Onias as high priest had the last say.

The high priest told him that there was such money laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children, and that some of it belonged to Hircanus son of Tobias, a man of great dignity, and not as that wicked Simon had misinformed: in all four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold. And that it was altogether impossible that such wrong should be done unto them that had committed it to the holiness of the place.

This Simon, having been a bewrayer of the money and of his country, slandered Onias, as if he had terrified Heliodorus and been the worker of these evils. He told the Greeks that Onias did that to Heliodorus. Thus was he bold to call him a traitor, that had deserved well of the city, and tendered his own nation, and was so zealous of the laws. He called that type of a brother a traitor.
Onias was an Israelite who sought the good of all, and Simon slandered him and his own factions committed murders; the Greeks were set against our nation and used Israelites to do it.

But when their hatred went so far, that by one of Simon's faction murders were committed: Simon hated Onias so much he had one of his men kill one of Onias's priests. That is why I say it is never just one thing; it is a domino effect of sins.

Onias, seeing the danger of this contention, and that Apollonius as governor of Coelosyria and Phenice did rage and increase Simon's malice, went to the king: not to be an accuser of his countrymen, but seeking the good of all, both public and private. He didn't even go there to accuse Simon. These are the characteristics of Onias III, a great and upstanding elder man.

For he saw that it was impossible that the state should continue quiet, and Simon leave his folly, unless the king did look thereunto. Blessed are the peacemakers, but peace does not always work with some people; some spirits are grimy, and at the end of the day they don't want peace with you.

source.name: TIPNR, Translators Individualised Proper Names with all References, by Tyndale House Cambridge, STEPBible.org
